parts.title: Arranging a school reunion
parts.context: A woman books a hotel for a school reunion dinner.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning a hotel to arrange a school reunion dinner. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: Riverside Hotel, Martin speaking. How can I help?

script.speaker: louise
script.text: Hello. I'm organising a reunion for people who left school twenty-five years ago, and I'd like to hold it at your hotel.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: That sounds like a lovely event. I'll take some details.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The event is a school reunion, so 'reunion' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: louise
script.text: Louise Pritchard. That's P-R-I-T-C-H-A-R-D.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: Thank you, Ms Pritchard. And when would you like to hold the event?

script.speaker: louise
script.text: On Saturday the fifteenth of November.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: I'll check the diary. Yes, that's free. How many guests do you expect?

script.speaker: louise
script.text: We invited fifty, but only forty have replied so far, so let's say forty.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: That fits comfortably in the Garden Suite, which holds up to sixty.

script.speaker: louise
script.text: Does it have a view of the river?

script.speaker: martin
script.text: It does, and it opens onto the terrace. What time would you like to start?

script.speaker: louise
script.text: Seven in the evening, so that people can get here after work.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: Now the food. For events like this, most people choose a hot buffet, with a choice of three main dishes, and a dessert table.

script.speaker: louise
script.text: That sounds right. Four of our guests are vegetarian, so we need a choice for them, too.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: Of course. We'll make sure there are two vegetarian dishes. The price is thirty-five pounds a head, and that includes a welcome drink.

script.speaker: louise
script.text: That's reasonable. What about the entertainment?

script.speaker: martin
script.text: Some groups bring their own music. Others hire a live band, and we can recommend a few. A band is more expensive than a DJ, but it gives the evening a lovely atmosphere.

script.speaker: louise
script.text: I'd like a band, if it plays songs from the nineties. That's what we listened to at school.

script.speaker: martin
script.text: I'll send you some names. One more thing: guests who stay overnight get a twenty percent discount on our rooms, if you tell us it's for the reunion.

script.speaker: louise
script.text: That's a very kind offer. Can you email me the details?

script.speaker: martin
script.text: Certainly. I'll send everything this afternoon.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A hotel staff induction
parts.context: A manager explains who does what to new hotel staff.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a hotel manager giving an induction talk to new staff. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: greco
script.text: Welcome to the Grand Hotel, everyone. I'm Sofia Greco, the human resources manager, and I'll explain how we work. The first thing is to know who does what, because guests will ask you for all kinds of things.

script.speaker: greco
script.text: If a guest wants help with luggage, that's the porters. They collect bags from the car and take them to the room, and they'll do the same when guests leave.

script.speaker: greco
script.text: If a guest orders food to their room, the order goes to the kitchen, and a waiter delivers it. We aim for twenty minutes, so don't promise anything faster.

script.speaker: greco
script.text: Complaints should always be passed to the duty manager. Even if you can solve the problem yourself, tell the manager, so that we can record it and learn from it.

script.speaker: greco
script.text: If someone has left something behind, it goes to housekeeping, who keep a book of lost property, and they'll hold items for three months.

script.speaker: greco
script.text: And if a guest asks about taxis, trains or restaurants, send them to the concierge, who knows the area very well. Reception handles check-in and check-out, and security looks after the building at night.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: greco
script.text: Now, a few rules. If a guest asks for something we can't provide, never just say no. Say you'll find someone who can help, and then do it, because that is what guests remember.

script.speaker: greco
script.text: Shifts are eight hours, with a thirty-minute break. Some people prefer a long shift, but we think eight is best for concentration.

script.speaker: greco
script.text: A meal is provided in the staff canteen during your break, and it's free. Please don't eat in the guest areas.

script.speaker: greco
script.text: Tips are shared among all staff, and not kept by the person who receives them. It's fairer, because the people who clean the rooms rarely meet the guests.

script.speaker: greco
script.text: Finally, your first morning. You'll start with safety training, which is compulsory and takes two hours. In the afternoon, you'll shadow an experienced colleague. Please wear your name badge at all times, and I'll see you on Monday.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A presentation on Impressionism
parts.context: Two art history students plan a presentation.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two art history students, Ella and Jamal, preparing a presentation on Impressionism. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: ella
script.text: Jamal, shall we plan our presentation on the Impressionists? We only have fifteen minutes, so we need to be selective.

script.speaker: jamal
script.text: Yes. I'd begin with what made them different. They painted outdoors, which wasn't usual at the time, because they wanted to catch the light as it changed.

script.speaker: ella
script.text: And their brushwork. They used short, thick strokes, which you can see on the canvas, instead of smooth, hidden brushwork.

script.speaker: jamal
script.text: Some people think they were praised immediately, but they weren't. Which painting shall we start with?

script.speaker: ella
script.text: 'Impression, Sunrise', by Monet, because the movement got its name from that painting. A critic used the word 'impression' as an insult.

script.speaker: jamal
script.text: Where was the first Impressionist exhibition held?

script.speaker: ella
script.text: In Paris in eighteen seventy-four, in a photographer's studio, which was an unusual place, because the artists were refused by the official exhibition.

script.speaker: jamal
script.text: What did the critics say at the time?

script.speaker: ella
script.text: That the paintings looked unfinished, like quick sketches, which was exactly the effect the painters wanted.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: ella
script.text: What do we say about Monet's later life? I know his paintings changed.

script.speaker: jamal
script.text: His eyesight got worse. He had cataracts, so he saw colours differently, and his late paintings are much redder and blurrier.

script.speaker: ella
script.text: How many slides can we have? Dr Perez said no more than twelve.

script.speaker: jamal
script.text: Twelve is plenty. I'll prepare a timeline, with the main exhibitions and dates, to put on the second slide.

script.speaker: ella
script.text: Good. And I'll prepare the handout, with a list of the paintings and where to see them.

script.speaker: jamal
script.text: When is the presentation? Is it Tuesday?

script.speaker: ella
script.text: No, Thursday, at two o'clock. So we should practise on Wednesday.

script.speaker: jamal
script.text: Good. Let's meet in the library at ten.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: how bridges carry loads
parts.context: An engineering lecture on types of bridges.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about how bridges carry loads. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Bridges are among the most visible examples of engineering, and today I want to explain the main types, and how each carries its load.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The simplest type is the beam bridge. It is just a horizontal beam resting on supports at each end. When a load, such as a lorry, crosses it, the top of the beam is squeezed, which is called compression, and the bottom is stretched, which is called tension. Beam bridges are cheap, but only suitable for short distances.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The arch bridge is much older. The Romans built arches of stone, and many are still standing after two thousand years. The curve of the arch turns the weight into compression, which stone resists very well. Arches work best for medium spans, because longer ones need enormous supports.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: For long distances, engineers use the suspension bridge. The roadway, or deck, hangs from steel cables, which are carried over tall towers and anchored at each end. The cables are in tension, and steel is very strong when pulled. The famous Golden Gate Bridge, in the American city of San Francisco, is a suspension bridge.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: A cable-stayed bridge looks similar, but the cables run straight from the towers to the deck, like the strings of a harp. It's cheaper than a suspension bridge for medium and long spans.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Wind is a serious danger. In nineteen forty, the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in the United States began to twist violently in a moderate wind, and collapsed. It was a lesson that engineers have never forgotten, and since then, designs have been tested in wind tunnels.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Today, new bridges are also tested using computer models, which can predict how a structure will behave under heavy traffic, strong winds and earthquakes, long before a single piece of steel is delivered. Next week we'll look at tunnels.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
